patient.name: Raymond Clarke
patient.complaint: Cramping pain in his right calf after walking about 200 yards, eased by stopping
background: Total cholesterol 6.8 mmol/L, not on a statin

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with exertional calf or buttock pain relieved by rest (intermittent claudication), with spinal stenosis, DVT and sciatica as distractors. Critical limb ischaemia (night rest pain eased by dangling the leg) and acute limb ischaemia (6 Ps) are the severe ends.

points: Raymond, 67, smoker with diabetes and hypertension.
**Cramping right calf pain** after about 200 yards.
Stops at the bus stop; pain goes in **2 to 3 minutes**.
Same distance every time; no pain at rest.

steps.lead: Raymond's calf pain on exertion fits atherosclerosis narrowing his **femoral artery**, the commonest site.
Raymond has all four risk factors, and **smoking** is the most important one to tackle.

steps.q: Raymond's pain is in his calf. Where is the disease most likely?
steps.r: **Calf** claudication = superficial femoral disease. **Buttock** claudication = iliac disease.

points: Right foot cool; **shiny, hairless skin** on the shin.
Right popliteal and foot pulses **absent**; femoral present.
Back exam normal; straight leg raise negative.

steps.lead: Raymond has textbook **intermittent claudication** plus the chronic ischaemic signs: absent pulses, cold limb, shiny skin, hair loss.
If Raymond's leg became **suddenly** pale and pulseless, that would be acute limb ischaemia: the 6 Ps.
If Raymond keeps smoking he may progress to **critical limb ischaemia**: rest pain at night, eased by dangling the leg off the bed.

visual.title: Duration of ischaemic rest pain
visual.label: Raymond: none
visual.caption: Rest pain for **over 2 weeks**, unrelieved by analgesia, defines critical limb ischaemia.

steps.text: Pain relieved by **sitting or bending forward** (not just standing still), with normal pulses, is spinal stenosis, not claudication.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (ABPI) and interpreting the ABPI value, then duplex ultrasound as first-line imaging. Watch for a falsely high ABPI in diabetes.

steps.q: What is the first test for Raymond in clinic?
steps.r: **ABPI** is first-line and part of the gold standard (ABPI plus imaging).

steps.title: Hand-held Doppler pressures
steps.text: ABPI = ankle systolic ÷ highest brachial systolic. Right 93 ÷ 150 = 0.62.

steps.lead: Raymond's right ABPI of **0.62** confirms PAD (below 0.9) but not severe (above 0.5). His left leg at 0.88 is mild.

visual.title: Raymond's right ABPI
visual.label: Raymond 0.62
visual.caption: Above **1.23** suggests calcified, non-compressible arteries (diabetes), not good flow.

steps.lead: Raymond goes on to **duplex ultrasound** to map the stenosis. MR angiography adds detail; CT angiography is for planning intervention.

points: Duplex: **70% stenosis** of the right superficial femoral artery.
Short segment; good run-off below the knee.

steps.lead: Raymond's **lipids and HbA1c** are checked: his cardiovascular risk matters as much as his leg.

steps.text: A **high** ABPI (over 1.23) in a diabetic is not reassuring. Calcified arteries resist cuff compression; image the arteries.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (supervised exercise, clopidogrel 75 mg and atorvastatin 80 mg, smoking cessation), then angioplasty if conservative treatment fails, bypass for long multifocal disease and amputation for irreversible infected critical ischaemia.

steps.q: What is the single most effective change Raymond can make?
steps.r: **Smoking** is the most important risk factor. Compression stockings are dangerous in arterial disease.

steps.lead: Raymond is referred for **supervised exercise** (2 hours a week for 3 months), starts **clopidogrel 75 mg** and **atorvastatin 80 mg**, and gets smoking cessation support.

visual.title: Raymond's walking distance
visual.caption: Supervised exercise builds collaterals: claudication distance more than doubles in 3 months.

steps.lead: If exercise had failed and his pain still limited his life, Raymond's short SFA stenosis would suit **angioplasty ± stent**.

steps.title: Stepwise PAD management
nodes: Risk factors: stop smoking, BP, diabetes, weight

steps.lead: Raymond's lesion is **short-segment**, so endovascular treatment fits. Long multifocal disease in a fit patient would need **open bypass**.
If Raymond ever developed acute limb ischaemia or critical ischaemia, he would need **urgent vascular referral**; an infected, irreversible limb means amputation.
Raymond's care follows **NICE CG147** on peripheral arterial disease.

steps.text: Clopidogrel, not aspirin, is the first-choice antiplatelet in symptomatic PAD; aspirin is the alternative if clopidogrel is unsuitable.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why exertion causes pain, why critical ischaemia causes rest pain and gangrene, why ABPI is falsely high in diabetes, and how exercise builds collaterals.

steps.lead: Raymond's narrowed SFA delivers enough blood at rest but not when his calf works harder, so pain appears at a **set distance**.
In critical ischaemia even **resting** flow fails: continuous pain, ulcers, gangrene. Dangling the leg helps because gravity adds pressure.
Raymond's diabetes could stiffen his arteries with calcium, so the cuff cannot compress them: a **falsely high ABPI**.
Raymond's clopidogrel and statin reduce **heart attack and stroke** risk; his exercise grows **collateral vessels** around the blockage.

steps.text: PAD is a marker of systemic atherosclerosis: most deaths are from **MI and stroke**, not the leg.

mcq.q: What is the most important risk factor for PAD?
Buttock claudication suggests disease in which vessel?
Which feature defines critical limb ischaemia?
mcq.r: Ischaemic **rest pain over 2 weeks**, often at night, relieved by dangling the leg.

mcq.q: Which is a sign of chronic limb ischaemia?
mcq.r: Absent pulses, cold limb, **shiny skin, hair loss**, ulcers.

mcq.q: Which ABPI range indicates severe PAD?
What is the first-line imaging investigation?
mcq.r: **Duplex ultrasound**; MRA third-line; CTA before intervention.

mcq.q: Which drugs are first-line in symptomatic PAD?
Which is second-line after conservative treatment fails?
Why is ABPI falsely high in diabetes?

technique.stem: A 64 year old man has a 6 month history of cramping pain in his left calf after walking about 150 yards. The pain settles within a few minutes of standing still. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day. The left foot is cool with absent pedal pulses and hair loss on the shin. Straight leg raise is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about exertional leg pain.

clues: cramping pain in his left calf after walking about 150 yards
settles within a few minutes of standing still
steps.x: Fixed walking distance, relief by standing still, smoker, absent pulses and trophic changes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: DVT gives a swollen warm leg not triggered by walking.
Spinal stenosis is eased by sitting or bending forward, with normal pulses.
Neuropathy causes burning, numb feet, not exertional cramp.
Sciatica shoots down the leg; straight leg raise is normal.

steps.x: **B. Intermittent claudication.** Rule: set distance, relieved by standing still, absent pulses.

technique.stem: A 70 year old woman has calf pain on walking 100 yards. Her brachial systolic pressure is 160 mmHg and her right ankle systolic pressure is 72 mmHg. She does not have diabetes.
technique.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of her ankle-brachial pressure index?

steps.x: It asks you to calculate and interpret the ABPI.
ABPI = 72 ÷ 160 = **0.45**. Non-diabetic, so the value is reliable.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Calcification gives an ABPI over 1.23.
Mild is 0.8–0.9.
0.5 to 0.8 would be moderate; hers is below 0.5.
Normal is 1.0–1.2.

steps.x: **E. Severe PAD.** Always calculate: ankle ÷ brachial.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man has intermittent claudication of the right calf at 200 yards. ABPI is 0.7 and duplex ultrasound shows a superficial femoral artery stenosis. He has stopped smoking. He is not taking any regular medication. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Supervised exercise with clopidogrel and atorvastatin

steps.x: Stable, not limb-threatening, no secondary prevention yet.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Amputation is for irreversible infected critical ischaemia.
Bypass is for long multifocal disease after conservative failure.
Angioplasty is second-line, after conservative treatment fails.
Anticoagulation is not used for stable PAD.

steps.x: **D.** Conservative first: exercise and best medical therapy.

technique.stem: A 68 year old man with claudication completes a 3 month supervised exercise programme. His pain-free walking distance increases from 150 yards to 400 yards. Repeat duplex ultrasound shows the superficial femoral artery stenosis is unchanged.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism for his improvement?

steps.x: A mechanism question: why walk further with the same stenosis?
Better function but the narrowing is unchanged, so blood is taking another route.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Exercise does not meaningfully raise Hb.
The stenosis is unchanged on duplex.
Vasoconstriction would worsen flow.
Exercise does not lyse plaque.

steps.x: **A. Collaterals.** Exercise works around the block, not through it.

practice.stem: A 71 year old man has a 1 year history of aching in his right calf that comes on after walking 100 yards and is relieved by standing still for 2 minutes. He smokes and has type 2 diabetes. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 156/90 mmHg. Right foot pulses are absent and the skin on the shin is shiny and hairless.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Exertional calf pain at a set distance relieved by rest, with absent pulses and trophic skin changes, is intermittent claudication from peripheral arterial disease.

steps.x: Set distance, rest relief, risk factors, absent pulses.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Baker's cyst is a popliteal swelling, not exertional pain.
Venous insufficiency gives oedema, varicosities and brown skin.
Spinal stenosis is relieved by sitting or bending forward; pulses normal.
Neuropathy is burning numbness, not exercise-related.

steps.x: **C.** Claudication = set distance + relief on standing still.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man has pain in both buttocks and thighs after walking 50 yards, relieved by standing still. He has erectile dysfunction. He smokes 30 cigarettes a day. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg. Both femoral pulses are weak.
practice.q: Which is the most likely site of arterial disease?
practice.e: Buttock claudication with weak femoral pulses indicates iliac (aorto-iliac) disease. Superficial femoral disease causes calf claudication.

steps.x: A site question: where is the narrowing?
Buttock pain and weak femoral pulses: disease is above the groin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Popliteal disease gives calf/foot pain with normal femorals.
Profunda disease alone rarely causes buttock pain.
SFA disease gives calf pain with normal femoral pulses.
Tibial disease causes foot pain.

practice.stem: A 76 year old woman with known peripheral arterial disease has had burning pain in her left foot every night for 4 weeks. It wakes her and is eased by hanging her leg over the side of the bed. Paracetamol and codeine do not help. There is a small black area on the tip of her second toe.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Ischaemic rest pain for over 2 weeks, worse at night and relieved by dangling the leg, with gangrene and ABPI under 0.5, is critical limb ischaemia.

steps.x: Diagnosis: which stage of arterial disease?

clues: hanging her leg over the side of the bed
steps.x: Rest pain over 2 weeks, eased by dependency, unrelieved by analgesia, gangrene.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Acute ischaemia is sudden (hours), with the 6 Ps.
Neuropathy is not relieved by dangling and ABPI would not be 0.32.
Gout is a hot swollen joint.
Claudication occurs on walking, not at rest.

steps.x: **B. Critical limb ischaemia.** Night rest pain + dangling relief.

practice.stem: A 69 year old man has had calf claudication for 2 years. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 150/84 mmHg. The doctor examines his legs.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the affected leg?
o: Cool foot with absent pedal pulses
practice.e: Chronic arterial insufficiency gives a cool limb with reduced or absent pulses, shiny skin, hair loss and ulcers. Haemosiderin staining and oedema are venous.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question in chronic PAD.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Bounding pulses mean good flow.
Haemosiderin staining is venous insufficiency.
Pitting oedema is venous or cardiac.
A warm red tender calf suggests DVT or cellulitis.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man has claudication of the left calf. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes and hypercholesterolaemia and smokes 25 cigarettes a day. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 146/88 mmHg. He asks which of his problems matters most for his legs.
practice.q: Which is the most important risk factor for his condition?
practice.e: Smoking is the most important risk factor for peripheral arterial disease; stopping is the most effective intervention.

steps.x: A risk factor question: which matters MOST?
All four risk factors present; the question asks for the most important.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Diabetes is a major risk factor but not the strongest.
Cholesterol matters but less than smoking.
Hypertension matters but less than smoking.
Male sex is non-modifiable and weaker.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man with peripheral arterial disease has a painful ulcer on the tip of his right big toe. It is small, deep, with a punched-out edge and a pale base. The foot is cool and pulses are absent. Elevation makes the pain worse. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 158/90 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely type of ulcer?
practice.e: Painful, punched-out ulcers on the toes with a pale base and absent pulses are arterial ulcers, a sign of progression to critical limb ischaemia.

clues: tip of his right big toe

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Marjolin's arises in a chronic scar or ulcer over years.
Neuropathic ulcers are painless, over pressure points, with a warm foot.
Pressure ulcers sit over heels and sacrum in immobile patients.
Venous ulcers are shallow, at the gaiter area, with oedema.

practice.stem: A 67 year old woman has a 4 month history of left calf pain on walking 150 yards, relieved by rest. She smokes. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 142/80 mmHg. Left foot pulses are weak.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: ABPI is the first-line investigation in suspected peripheral arterial disease and part of the gold standard (ABPI plus imaging).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: CTA is for planning intervention.
DSA is invasive, used during intervention.
MRA is third-line.
Venous duplex looks for DVT.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes has calf pain on walking 100 yards. His foot pulses are difficult to feel. ABPI is measured and the arteries at the ankle cannot be compressed by the cuff.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: Duplex ultrasound of the leg arteries
practice.e: ABPI over 1.23 in diabetes reflects calcified, non-compressible arteries and is unreliable. Duplex ultrasound is the first-line imaging to confirm PAD.

steps.x: The next test when the ABPI cannot be trusted.
Claudication with a falsely high ABPI from calcification.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Coronary angiography tests the heart, not the legs.
Nerve studies test neuropathy, not exertional pain.
Repeating an unreliable test delays diagnosis.
Spine X-ray does not assess arteries.

steps.x: **B. Duplex ultrasound.** ABPI >1.23 = calcified, not normal.

practice.stem: A 65 year old woman has calf claudication at 200 yards. ABPI is 0.72. She has stopped smoking and is not taking any medication. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate drug treatment?
practice.e: Symptomatic PAD needs clopidogrel 75 mg once daily and atorvastatin 80 mg, with supervised exercise. Anticoagulation is not first-line.

steps.x: Symptomatic PAD, no antiplatelet or statin yet.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Aspirin is second choice and simvastatin 20 mg is not high intensity.
Naftidrofuryl is only considered later if exercise fails.
Full-dose DOAC is not first-line.
Warfarin is not used for stable PAD.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man has right calf claudication at 50 yards that stops him working. He completed 3 months of supervised exercise and takes clopidogrel and atorvastatin, but there is no improvement. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 134/78 mmHg. Duplex shows a short-segment stenosis of the right superficial femoral artery.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: When conservative management fails and symptoms affect quality of life, a short-segment stenosis is treated by percutaneous transluminal angioplasty with or without stent.

steps.x: Next step after conservative treatment fails.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Amputation is for irreversible infected critical ischaemia.
He has already failed an adequate trial.
Heparin is for acute ischaemia.
Sympathectomy is not standard treatment.

steps.x: **D. Angioplasty.** Short lesion = endovascular; long multifocal = bypass.

practice.stem: An 81 year old man with critical limb ischaemia of the left leg has a black, foul-smelling forefoot with spreading cellulitis to the ankle. Vascular imaging shows no option for revascularisation. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Oral antibiotics and review in 2 weeks
practice.e: Irreversible critical limb ischaemia with superimposed infection is managed by below-knee amputation once revascularisation is not possible.

steps.x: Definitive management of an unsalvageable, infected limb.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Compression worsens arterial flow.
Imaging shows no bypass target.
Delay risks sepsis and death.
Exercise is for claudication.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman with type 2 diabetes for 20 years has calf pain on walking. Her foot pulses are faint. Her ABPI is unexpectedly high. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 148/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her ABPI result?
o: Calcified arterial walls that cannot be compressed
practice.e: In diabetes, medial arterial calcification makes vessels non-compressible, giving a falsely elevated ABPI over 1.23.

steps.x: A mechanism question: why is the ABPI high?
Symptoms of PAD but a high reading: the test is fooled.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No fistula in the history.
High output does not selectively raise ankle pressure.
Faint pulses and claudication contradict normal flow.
Autonomic neuropathy does not explain a non-compressible cuff reading.

prompts.q: What is peripheral arterial disease and what are its risk factors?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the most important risk factor.

points.p: Atherosclerosis of peripheral (usually lower limb) arteries, reduced flow
points.why: A marker of systemic vascular disease.
Stopping is the biggest single intervention.

prompts.q: Describe intermittent claudication and how the pain site localises disease.

points.p: Cramping leg pain after a set distance, relieved by rest
points.why: Spinal stenosis is relieved by sitting forward.

prompts.q: What examination findings suggest chronic limb ischaemia?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: arterial vs venous signs.

points.why: Feel femoral, popliteal and foot pulses.

prompts.q: What defines critical limb ischaemia and how does it differ from acute limb ischaemia?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: weeks of rest pain vs hours of 6 Ps.

points.p: Rest pain over 2 weeks, often at night, unrelieved by analgesia
Relieved by dangling the leg off the bed

prompts.q: What is the first-line investigation and how do you interpret the ABPI?

points.p: ABPI first-line (gold standard ABPI plus imaging)

prompts.q: Which imaging tests are used, in what order?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: duplex, MRA, then CTA before intervention.

points.p: Lipids and HbA1c for CV risk

prompts.q: What is the first-line management of intermittent claudication?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: exercise, drugs, risk factors, with doses.

points.p: Smoking cessation, BP, diabetes and weight control

prompts.q: What are the next steps if conservative treatment fails, and in emergencies?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: lesion length and patient risk decide the procedure.

points.p: Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty ± stent (short segment, high risk)
Open bypass graft for long-segment/multifocal disease in low-risk patients
points.why: Ilio-femoral bypass for external iliac/proximal femoral disease.

points.p: Urgent vascular referral for acute or critical ischaemia
Below-knee amputation for irreversible infected CLI
points.why: When the limb cannot be saved.

prompts.q: Why does exertion cause claudication, and why does critical ischaemia cause rest pain?

points.p: Plaque narrows the artery, so flow cannot rise to meet exercising muscle demand
In CLI, resting flow is inadequate: continuous pain, ulcers, gangrene

prompts.q: Why is ABPI falsely high in diabetes, and why do statins, antiplatelets and exercise help?

points.p: Arterial wall calcification makes vessels non-compressible: ABPI >1.23
Clopidogrel and statins reduce CV risk and slow atherosclerosis
points.why: Most deaths are MI and stroke.

glossary.PAD: Peripheral arterial disease: atherosclerotic narrowing of limb arteries.
glossary.Intermittent claudication: Cramping leg pain after walking a set distance, relieved by rest.
glossary.Critical limb ischaemia: Ischaemic rest pain over 2 weeks, ulcers or gangrene; the limb is threatened.
glossary.Acute limb ischaemia: Sudden loss of limb blood supply, presenting with the 6 Ps.
glossary.6 Ps: Pain, pulselessness, pallor, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishing cold.
glossary.Rest pain: Ischaemic pain in the foot at rest, often at night, when flow is inadequate even without exercise.
glossary.Superficial femoral artery: The main thigh artery; stenosis causes calf claudication.
glossary.Iliac: The pelvic arteries; disease here causes buttock claudication.
glossary.ABPI: Ankle-brachial pressure index: ankle systolic divided by brachial systolic pressure.
glossary.Duplex ultrasound: Ultrasound combining images and Doppler flow; first-line imaging for PAD.
glossary.MR angiography: MRI of the arteries with contrast, giving anatomical detail.
glossary.CT angiography: Contrast CT of the arteries, used to plan intervention.
glossary.Collateral vessels: Small alternative arteries that grow around a blockage.
glossary.Arterial calcification: Calcium in the artery wall making it stiff and non-compressible.
glossary.Non-compressible: An artery the BP cuff cannot squeeze shut, giving a falsely high reading.
glossary.Clopidogrel: An antiplatelet drug blocking the P2Y12 receptor; first-line in PAD at 75 mg daily.
glossary.Atorvastatin: A high-intensity statin given at 80 mg to lower cholesterol and CV risk.
glossary.Angioplasty: Widening a narrowed artery with a balloon via a catheter, often with a stent.
glossary.Stent: A mesh tube left in an artery to keep it open.
glossary.Endovascular: Treatment from inside the vessel through a catheter.
glossary.Bypass graft: A vein or synthetic tube routing blood around a blocked artery.
glossary.Ilio-femoral bypass: A graft from the iliac artery to the femoral artery.
glossary.Below-knee amputation: Removal of the leg below the knee for an unsalvageable limb.
glossary.Gangrene: Death of tissue from lost blood supply; black and shrunken.
glossary.Arterial ulcer: Painful, punched-out ulcer on the toes or foot from poor arterial supply.
glossary.Trophic changes: Shiny skin, hair loss and thick nails from long-term poor blood supply.
glossary.Spinal stenosis: Narrowing of the spinal canal causing leg pain on walking, relieved by sitting or bending forward.
glossary.Haemosiderin: Iron pigment staining the skin brown in venous disease.
glossary.HbA1c: Glycated haemoglobin, showing average blood glucose over about 3 months.
glossary.Supervised exercise: Structured walking programme, 2 hours a week for 3 months, first-line for claudication.
